strengths: Novel unified framework using probabilistic circuits for MTP, enabling systematic exploration of architecture design space with both existing (FF, CP) and new (HMM, BTree) variants
Introduces two new MTP architectures (HMM and BTree) that are well-motivated and empirically validated, advancing the state of MTP design
Comprehensive experimental methodology with thorough ablations addressing three research questions, multiple GPU evaluation (L40S and RTX 3090), and proper error reporting across runs
Technically sound approach to speculative decoding with quality guarantees and an efficient self-drafting mechanism (Algorithm 2) that reuses shared backbone state
Strong reproducibility: code provided, full algorithmic details, public dataset (Tulu 3), complete hyperparameter specifications, and proper statistical analysis
Systematic two-dimensional tradeoff analysis examining both PC architecture choice and LoRA layer sharing, with device-specific insights that are practically useful
Clear presentation with effective visualizations (especially iso-throughput lines in Figure 1) and accessible writing that manages conceptual complexity well
Meaningful speedups demonstrated (5.47× over AR generation, 1.22× over existing MTP methods) with principled optimization of the expressiveness-efficiency frontier
weaknesses: Severely limited evaluation scope: only single model (EvaByte) and single model family (byte-level LLMs) tested, undermining generality claims and comparison with prior work like Basharin et al. (2025) on subword models with larger vocabularies

Modest practical gains over MTP baseline: 1.22× speedup is meaningful but not dramatic, with relative improvements of 13-27% depending on configuration, raising questions about complexity-benefit tradeoff

Incomplete experimental coverage: only two window sizes (n=8,16) explored despite motivation around efficiency-expressiveness tradeoff, no design space exploration, and only instruction fine-tuning evaluation on Tulu 3

Mixed results for HMM architecture: despite highest acceptance rates, HMM suffers worst latency (0.0397 vs 0.0322 for CP), resulting in lower throughput, and this architectural mismatch with motivation is not deeply analyzed

Conservative initialization strategy that guarantees smooth training but may limit exploration: initializing HMM/CP equivalent to FF at start prevents learning of significantly different distributions, and this design choice lacks ablation studies

Incomplete training data details: acknowledged limitation that 'full details of the data mix are not known and hard to replicate'; training only on Tulu 3 subset, not full EvaByte-SFT mix; filtered validation set (English-only, no EOS) confounds results

LoRA layer tradeoffs add complexity without consistent benefits: additional layers increase acceptance but can decrease throughput (Table 3), with device-specific optimal configurations, potentially limiting practical adoption

Limited analysis of architectural choices: insufficient investigation into why CP excels for n=8 and BTree for n=16; no error analysis, qualitative investigation, or visualization of learned mixture structures and HMM transitions

Vocabulary size dependency: small byte vocabulary (320) makes approach tractable but scalability to larger vocabularies (v ≥ 100k) unclear; no scaling analysis provided despite acknowledged challenges in prior work

No downstream task evaluation: paper measures only generation speed and token acceptance rates, with no assessment of whether improved expressiveness translates to better language understanding or task performance

strengths: Principled probabilistic circuits framework that elegantly unifies FF, CP, HMM, and BTree architectures with sound mathematical foundations (smoothness, decomposability)
Comprehensive experimental design with systematic ablations across mixture components, window sizes, LoRA layers, and multiple GPUs, enabling clear characterization of trade-offs
Technically solid integration of speculative decoding with practical optimization (Algorithm 2) for reusing shared LLM states
Honest treatment of expressiveness-latency trade-offs with clear visualization of the Pareto frontier, avoiding overclaiming
Reproducibility efforts including detailed algorithms, training specifications, and code provision
weaknesses: Limited novelty: applies established PC theory (Choi et al. 2020) and known tensor factorizations to MTP; the contribution is primarily engineering rather than methodological innovation

Modest empirical improvements of 1.22× over FF baseline (Table 3, n=16), with even smaller gains for n=8; the 5.47× speedup vs. STP conflates window size benefits (n=8 pretraining) with expressiveness improvements

Severely restricted evaluation scope: single byte-level model (EvaByte) with no subword evaluation despite acknowledging byte-level LLMs represent niche use cases; no direct comparison with Basharin et al. (2025) on comparable settings
Overstated claims: the 'guarantee to retain performance' (abstract/intro) is standard speculative decoding used by prior work (Cai et al., Zheng et al., Basharin et al.); not novel to this work
Hardware-dependent optimal configurations: L40S works best with 2 LoRA layers, RTX 3090 with 1 (Tables 3 vs 6), undermining generalizability; latency overhead of LoRA becomes prohibitive quickly

Incomplete experimental setup: EvaByte pre-trained for n=8 but retrofitted for n=16 without design intent; training limited to 2 epochs and 8192 byte context due to 'GPU constraints'; data mix incomplete

Insufficient architectural analysis: limited intuition for architecture selection (e.g., why BTree outperforms HMM beyond vague 'non-autoregressive' claim); why Basharin et al. required MoE-specific losses but this work claims otherwise is unexplained
Dense presentation with critical results relegated to appendices (loss comparison in G, HMM ablations in E); central Figure 2 difficult to parse despite importance
Some performance differences within noise margins (e.g., CP vs BTree for n=8: 200.9±1.6 vs 196.6±3.8 tokens/s); limited cross-domain evaluation
Reproducibility limitations despite stated efforts: training context constrained by GPU availability; incomplete data specifications; no pre-trained model releases

strengths: Novel and theoretically grounded framework: Probabilistic circuits provide an elegant, principled way to unify and generalize MTP approaches (FF, CP, HMM, BTree), moving beyond ad-hoc architectures. The PC framework with smoothness and decomposability properties is technically sound.

Strong empirical methodology: Thorough ablation studies (RQ1-RQ3), evaluation on two different GPUs with consistent results, multiple runs with statistical reporting, and fair comparisons (same training steps as baselines).

Quality guarantees via speculative decoding: Unlike prior MTP work that sacrifices quality, this approach maintains the original model's generation quality exactly (greedy) or in expectation (sampling), with well-designed self-speculative decoding algorithm.

Substantial practical speedup: 5.47× over autoregressive generation and 1.22× over standard MTP is meaningful for deployment; detailed tradeoff analysis (Tables 1-3) provides actionable insights on configuration choices.
Excellent reproducibility: Code provided, complete training details, clear metric definitions, hyperparameter justification, and comprehensive algorithms in appendices.

Clear presentation and motivation: The 'Cape Town/Pretoria/Cretoria' example effectively motivates the problem; Figure 2 elegantly visualizes the spectrum of PC architectures; generally well-written throughout.
weaknesses: Limited evaluation scope: Evaluation restricted to a single model (EvaByte, 6.5B parameters) and single token granularity (bytes). No evaluation on other byte-level models (MambaByte, ByteNet) or subword-token models, limiting claims about generality of the PC framework. No direct head-to-head comparison with recent speculative decoding methods (EAGLE, Hydra).

Hardware-dependent optimal configurations: Different LoRA layer counts optimal on different GPUs (1 on RTX 3090, 2 on L40S), indicating configuration sensitivity. No principled method provided for selecting optimal settings on new hardware, complicating deployment.

Modest improvements over MTP: The 1.22× speedup over independent FF baseline is meaningful but incremental. Acceptance rate improvements ~0.8 tokens (5.94 vs 5.14) diminish quickly, with n=8 hitting diminishing returns.

Incomplete scalability analysis: Only window sizes n=8 and n=16 tested; behavior for larger windows (n=32, 64) unexplored. Acceptance rate scaling with window size not thoroughly analyzed. Only small-to-medium model tested (6.5B).

Limited architectural guidance: No principled analysis of when to choose which PC architecture; HMM selected over BTree empirically due to latency despite better acceptance rates. No ablation on PC structural properties (depth vs. width). Architecture selection appears ad-hoc.

Missing practical considerations: No analysis of training cost compared to baselines; energy consumption not discussed; limited error analysis on when/why architectures fail; only 250 prompts for evaluation (could use standard benchmarks); validation set only 1% (very small for tuning).

strengths: Technically sound methodology with proper formal guarantees through speculative decoding (greedy = identical, sampling = matches in expectation)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple dimensions: 4 circuit architectures, mixture components (r∈{8-128}), window sizes (8,16), LoRA layers (0-4), and two GPU architectures
Practical speedups of 5.15× for EvaByte-6.5B and 2.24× for Llama 3.2 3B Byte over AR, with 1.17× over independence-assumption MTP methods
Novel application of probabilistic circuits to MTP with new architectures (HMM, BTree) for byte-level models, unifying FF/CP approaches
Rigorous systematic analysis of expressiveness-latency trade-offs in two dimensions (PC architecture and layer sharing)
Clear presentation with strong visualizations (Figs 1-2), intuitive examples (byte-salad problem), and comprehensive appendices supporting reproducibility
Self-speculative decoding design with state sharing elegantly reduces overhead to single LLM forward pass per cycle
Honest limitations discussion acknowledging batch size, language, memory scaling constraints
weaknesses: Missing empirical comparison with primary baselines: Hydra and EAGLE are acknowledged as state-of-the-art MTP methods but not directly compared; Appendix D provides theoretical justification but no experiments validate claims about vocabulary size/window size differences limiting shallow AR applicability

Limited evaluation scope: English-only evaluation despite byte-level models' multilingual capabilities; EvaByte known to switch languages with high variance; acknowledged in limitations but undermines generalizability

Memory bottleneck for subword models unresolved: Table 5 shows 250GB+ requirements for v=128k, n=16, r=32; proposed solutions (subsampling, parameter sharing) not implemented; severely limits claimed generality beyond byte-level models
Batch size 1 only: All experiments at batch size 1 to isolate trade-off effects; unrealistic for production deployment and potentially changes optimal architecture choices

Modest improvements over prior MTP methods: 1.17× speedup over independence-assumption MTP is meaningful but not transformational; most gains in sampling regime rather than greedy decoding; for EvaByte greedy decoding, FF actually outperforms expressive circuits (Table 11)
No downstream task evaluation: Only throughput metrics reported; quality preservation through speculative decoding not validated on actual generation tasks (summarization, translation, QA)
Artificial experimental constraints: EOS token restriction to prevent length-based gaming; 1% validation split; filtering to English-only examples reduces dataset representativeness
Limited theoretical analysis: No formal characterization of expressiveness-latency trade-off; empirical only; no analysis of why HMM incurs high latency versus BTree

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing realistic limitations of independence assumptions in MTP
Principled unification of multiple MTP approaches under probabilistic circuits framework
Technically sound with proper theoretical grounding and efficient sampling algorithms
Comprehensive systematic evaluation across multiple architectures, window sizes, and configurations
Quality guarantees through speculative decoding that match original LLM outputs
Honest and transparent discussion of limitations (batch size, languages, memory, scalability)
Reproducibility commitment with detailed algorithmic descriptions in appendices
weaknesses: Severely limited scope: byte-level LLMs only; not extensible to mainstream subword models due to prohibitive memory costs (Table 5)
Cannot extend to subword vocabularies: logits memory scales as s×n×v×r, reaching 250GB+ for reasonable settings (unresolved)
Modest empirical gains over independence baseline: only 1.17× speedup despite added complexity
Missing empirical comparison with state-of-the-art MTP methods (Hydra, EAGLE); post-hoc justifications in Appendix D insufficient
Experimental constraints severely limit generalizability: batch size 1 only, English-only generation, EOS token restrictions
Complex design space with multiple hyperparameters (architecture, r, LoRA layers, window size) requiring model-specific tuning; no principled selection guidance
Limited novelty: probabilistic circuits are established; individual PC architectures are straightforward instantiations
Figure 1 difficult to interpret; unclear how practitioners should use the framework
Key design choices lack justification (why n≤16? why γ=0.9?)
Limited statistical analysis and no significance testing; some results within error margins

strengths: Novel application of probabilistic circuits to multi-token prediction with unified framework elegantly covering FF, CP, HMM, and BTree architectures
Thorough experimental evaluation: 55 models trained with systematic exploration of two tradeoff dimensions (PC architecture and LoRA layers)
Strong practical results: 5.15× speedup over autoregressive generation on EvaByte with guaranteed output quality via speculative decoding
Honest and comprehensive treatment of limitations including memory bottlenecks, batch size constraints, and subword scalability issues
Well-motivated problem framing (byte-salad continuations) and clear presentation with informative figures demonstrating expressiveness-latency tradeoffs
New MTP architectures (HMM, BTree) shown to outperform existing approaches, particularly for larger prediction windows (n=16)
weaknesses: Missing empirical comparison with state-of-the-art MTP methods (EAGLE, Hydra) on byte-level models; Appendix D provides only theoretical arguments rather than validation
Modest improvement over baseline MTP with independence assumptions (1.17×), particularly when considering that greedy decoding sometimes favors simpler MTPC-FF over more expressive architectures
Critical scalability limitation to subword models due to memory bottleneck for logits (vocabulary size 32k requires ~250GB); proposed mitigations in Appendix G are untested

Design choices lack principled justification: HMM configuration choices appear empirically driven, LoRA layer selection not systematically explored, exponential discounting parameter motivation unclear

Incomplete analysis: no empirical demonstration that MTPC avoids byte-salad problems, limited testing across model sizes (only 6.5B and 3B), high measurement variability not fully characterized (e.g., ±13.3 tok/s)

Technical clarity: partition function complexity O(|c|) needs explicit statement; throughput metric uses ratio of means rather than mean of ratio with unquantified error; Algorithm 2's interaction with LoRA gradient flow under-explained
